o: Find the box with the smallest capacity that is still at least itemSize; ties broken by smallest index. Example 1: capacities [1,5,3,7], item 3 -> box 2 (capacity 3). Example 2: capacities 3 and 3 tie, so index 0 wins. Example 3: nothing fits, return -1. With at most 100 boxes, a single linear scan is trivially sufficient.
k: One pass tracking the best (smallest fitting) capacity and its index; strict '<' comparison preserves the earliest index on ties.

a.i: Iterate through boxes; whenever capacity[i] >= itemSize and it beats the current best capacity, update best index. Strict inequality keeps the first index among ties.
s: For each i: if capacity[i] >= itemSize and (best == -1 or capacity[i] < capacity[best]), set best = i.
a.t: O(n) — one pass over the boxes.

a.n: Approach 2: Sort a copy of (capacity, index) pairs
a.i: Sort boxes by capacity (ties by index), then return the first box whose capacity fits. More overhead, but illustrates the 'sort and pick first feasible' pattern useful when the array must stay untouched or repeated queries arrive.
s: Create pairs (capacity[i], i) and sort them.
Scan sorted pairs; return the index of the first with capacity >= itemSize.
a.t: O(n log n) — dominated by sorting.

w: Use the linear scan; sorting is unnecessary work for a one-shot query. Pitfall: using '<=' instead of '<' when updating the best, which breaks the tie-breaking rule. Edge cases: all boxes too small (-1), item fits every box (index of the global minimum). Follow-up: answer many itemSize queries efficiently (preprocess sorted capacities plus a first-fit lookup).
